claims.text: The five-element Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy has a more heterogeneous local chemical environment than its quaternary and ternary subsets.
The full five-element mixture has enhanced lattice distortion and chemical short-range order relative to the simpler subsets.
Local chemical order and lattice distortion alter the stacking-fault-energy landscape.
Changes in stacking fault energy can shift the onset of deformation twinning.
Local stacking-fault-energy fluctuations and lattice distortion impede dislocation glide.
Dislocation activity and deformation twinning affect sustained strain hardening and resistance to plastic instability.
The quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys in the comparison are all single-phase FCC materials after thermomechanical processing.
Constituent count will be reduced from five to four and three while processing, grain size, and FCC phase structure are held unchanged.
The quinary alloy has more pronounced local fluctuations in stacking fault energy than the quaternary and ternary subsets.
The quinary alloy initiates deformation twinning later than the quaternary and ternary subsets.
Reduced chemical complexity produces a more uniform stacking-fault-energy landscape in the quaternary and ternary alloys.
Relative to the quinary baseline, the quaternary and ternary alloys will begin deformation twinning at lower strain.
Relative to the quinary baseline, the quaternary and ternary alloys will have lower work-hardening rates.
Relative to the quinary baseline, the quaternary and ternary alloys will have reduced strength and/or ductility.
The quinary baseline exhibits delayed twin initiation and strong strain hardening that enhance its strength and ductility.
The proposed comparison applies to room-temperature, quasi-static uniaxial tensile loading.
Subtle grain-size variations and residual stresses could also affect the measured behavior and must be controlled.
Failure to observe earlier twinning or reduced work hardening in the subsets, or failure to detect complexity-associated SFE differences, would falsify the hypothesis.
